Declares that preventing genocide and other atrocities is a national interest of the United States and requires the executive branch to organize, train, and report accordingly.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: Pub. L. 115-441](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/115/public/441){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 22 U.S.C. 2656 note](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/22/2656?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Statement of policy that atrocity prevention is a core national security interest.
- Training for Foreign Service officers posted to countries at risk.
- Annual report to Congress on atrocity risks and the government's response, coordinated by an interagency body.

## Why it matters

It gave statutory backing to the interagency atrocity prevention structure first set up in 2012. It is usually read together with the [Global Fragility Act](gfa-2019.qmd), since both push the government toward early warning and prevention.

## Current status

In force. The annual reporting requirement had an initial six-year term.

[Last checked November 10, 2026.]{.checked}

## Where it sits

- **Layer.** Specific authorization. Laws aimed at a particular conflict, country, program, or problem. Most work through a framework statute: an AUMF through the War Powers Resolution, a sanctions act through IEEPA. ([How the layers work](../study/index.qmd#the-authority-stack))
- **Codified in.** [Title 22 U.S.C.](title22-usc.qmd).
- **Era.** Sanctions, cyber, and great powers ([timeline](../study/timeline.qmd)).
- **Study.** [Unit 10: Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners](../study/units/assistance.qmd) (core reading); [Unit 12: Civilian harm and the conduct of operations](../study/units/civilian-harm.qmd) (further reading).
